summary: Morocco lies at the northwestern corner of Africa, facing Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar. It blends Arab, Berber and European cultures and is known for its old cities, deserts and cuisine.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam arrived in the late 7th and 8th centuries with the Arab conquest, and spread among the Berber tribes after the Idrisid dynasty was founded in 789. In the 11th–12th centuries the Berber dynasties of the Almoravids and Almohads established the Maliki school of Sunni Islam as orthodoxy, and Sufi orders and saint veneration also penetrated the countryside. Today the king, as "Commander of the Faithful", is the supreme religious authority, the constitution makes Islam the state religion, and almost all citizens are Muslims.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: There were Christian communities in North Africa in Roman times, but they almost disappeared after Islamization. During the French and Spanish protectorate of 1912–1956, large numbers of European immigrants brought Catholicism, and most left after independence. Today's Christians are mainly foreign residents and immigrants from sub-Saharan Africa, and Moroccan citizens who convert to Christianity still face social pressure.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Moroccan society is strongly religious, and openly declaring no religion brings social and legal pressure, so very few people explicitly call themselves non-religious, mainly highly educated young people in cities; in recent years polls show that religiosity among the younger generation has declined.

religion.background: The indigenous Berbers (Amazigh) of Morocco partly accepted Christianity and Judaism in Roman times. At the end of the 7th century and the beginning of the 8th, Arab armies conquered North Africa, and in 789 Idris I founded the Idrisid dynasty, after which Islam gradually spread among the Berber tribes. In the 11th–12th centuries the Almoravid and Almohad dynasties founded by Berbers united the Maghreb and southern Iberia and established the Maliki school of Sunni Islam as orthodoxy. The present Alaouite dynasty has ruled since the 17th century, and the king also holds the title of "Commander of the Faithful" (Amir al-Mu'minin), the religious authority of the state. Historically Morocco had the largest Jewish community in North Africa, and after the founding of Israel in 1948 most emigrated to Israel, France and Canada.

language.official: Arabic and Berber (Amazigh) are the official languages.

ranking.name: Moroccan Arabic (Darija)
ranking.description: Moroccan Arabic (Darija) is a dialect formed through long contact between Arabic and Berber, and it has absorbed French and Spanish vocabulary, differing greatly from the Arabic of the Middle East. It is the main everyday language of Moroccan cities and plains and the common language among the various peoples, while formal writing uses Modern Standard Arabic.

ranking.name: Tashelhit
ranking.description: Tashelhit is the most widely spoken Berber language in Morocco, found mainly in the Souss Valley in the southwest, the Anti-Atlas and the western High Atlas. These mountain areas have rugged terrain and were less affected by Arabization, so the Berber language was preserved. After the 2011 constitution recognized Amazigh as an official language, schools also began teaching the Tifinagh script.

ranking.name: Central Atlas Tamazight
ranking.description: Central Atlas Tamazight is found in the Middle Atlas and eastern High Atlas of central Morocco, and its speakers are mostly Berber tribes who traditionally lived by herding. These tribes fiercely resisted the French colonial army in the 1930s.

ranking.name: Tarifit
ranking.description: Tarifit is the Berber language of the northern Rif mountains. The Rif region was part of the Spanish protectorate from 1912 to 1956, and from 1921 to 1926 Abd el-Krim led the Republic of the Rif here in resistance against Spain and France. After independence relations between the area and the central government were tense, and large numbers of residents emigrated to the Netherlands and Belgium.

language.history: The earliest language of Morocco was Berber (Amazigh); after the Arab conquest at the end of the 7th century, Arabic came to the cities with Islam; in the 12th century the Almohad dynasty moved Arab tribes into the Atlantic plains, and Arabization gradually spread to the countryside. During the French and Spanish protectorate of 1912–1956, French became the language of administration, education and commerce, while Spanish was used in the north. After independence an "Arabization" policy was pursued and Berber was long suppressed; in 2001 King Mohammed VI established the Royal Institute of Amazigh Culture, and in 2011 the new constitution made Amazigh an official language alongside Arabic.

ranking.name: Tagine
ranking.description: Lamb, chicken or vegetables slowly stewed in a clay pot with a conical lid, with preserved lemon, olives, plums or apricots added, and seasoned with saffron, cumin and cinnamon.
ranking.history: The name tagine refers both to the dish and to the clay pot; the conical lid lets steam condense and flow back, allowing stewing with little water in water-scarce North Africa. This stewing method is generally thought to originate with the Berbers, and from the 9th century, influenced by Arab and Abbasid cuisine, fruits and spices were added, forming a style blending sweet and savory. After the 15th century Muslims and Jews returning from Al-Andalus also brought more cooking techniques. Today tagine is an everyday dish in every Moroccan household.

ranking.name: Couscous
ranking.description: Coarse wheat semolina rolled into tiny granules and steamed, topped with stewed meat and seven vegetables. It has a fluffy texture, absorbs the aroma of the stew sauce, and is often accompanied by a fermented milk drink.
ranking.history: Couscous is a traditional staple of the Berbers, and its earliest written records appear in 13th-century cookbooks. In Morocco, Friday is the Muslim day of congregational prayer, and after worship families eat couscous together, also giving some to mosques and the poor. In 2020 couscous, jointly nominated by Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Mauritania, was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list.

ranking.name: Pastilla
ranking.description: A pie of paper-thin warqa pastry filled with pigeon (or chicken), almonds, eggs and spices and baked, dusted on top with powdered sugar and cinnamon, both sweet and savory.
ranking.history: Pastilla is generally thought to be connected with the court cuisine of Al-Andalus (medieval Muslim-ruled Spain); after the fall of Granada in 1492, large numbers of Muslims and Jews fled to Moroccan cities such as Fez and Tetouan, bringing this kind of refined cuisine. It is the signature dish of Fez, takes time to make, and often appears at weddings and important festivals, with the pigeon version regarded as the most authentic.

ranking.name: Harira soup
ranking.description: A thick soup cooked from tomatoes, lentils, chickpeas, lamb and herbs, thickened with flour or egg. It has a rich flavor with the aroma of herbs and spices, and is often eaten with dates.
ranking.history: Harira is the most important soup for breaking the fast during Ramadan in Morocco; the first meal after sunset usually begins with dates, milk and a bowl of harira. It is nutritious and replenishes energy after a long fast. The harira recipe differs across Morocco and from family to family, and the recipe is often a family tradition passed from mother to daughter.

ranking.name: Msemen (layered flatbread)
ranking.description: A square layered flatbread made by repeatedly oiling and folding dough and frying it on a griddle, often drizzled with honey or eaten with tea. It is crisp outside and layered inside, and can be sweet or savory.
ranking.history: Msemen is one of the most common breakfast and afternoon-tea snacks in Morocco, and the method of making it has long been passed down in North Africa, with similar pancakes also found in Algeria and Tunisia. During Ramadan it is a common food on the iftar table, and street stalls sell it from early morning, enjoyed together with Moroccan mint tea.
